title.zh: 第十三 五行一 貌不恭 淫雨 服妖 雞禍 青眚 屋自壞 訛言 旱 謠 狼食人
title.raw: 第十三 五行一 貌不恭 淫雨 服妖 雞禍 青眚 屋自壞 訛言 旱 謠 狼食人 Volume 103: Five Elements Part One

sentences.zh: 志第十三 五行一

translations.literal: Treatise, the thirteenth: Five Elements, part one.
translations.idiomatic: Treatise Thirteen: The Five Elements, Part One.

sentences.zh: 貌不恭 淫雨 服妖 雞禍 青眚 屋自壞 訛言 旱 謠 狼食人

translations.literal: Lack of dignity in demeanor; excessive rain; clothing prodigies; chicken disasters; green calamities; houses collapsing of themselves; false rumors; drought; songs and portents; wolves devouring people.
translations.idiomatic: Undignified bearing; unseasonable downpours; dress as ill omen; calamities involving fowl; greenish spectral blights; dwellings that fall without human cause; lying rumors; drought; rhymed portents; wolves that prey on men.

sentences.zh: 《五行傳》說及其占應，《漢書·五行志》錄之詳矣。

translations.literal: The Treatise on the Five Elements sets forth the theory together with its divination and corresponding events; the "Treatise on the Five Elements" in the Book of Han recorded these in detail.
translations.idiomatic: The classic exposition in the Treatise on the Five Elements, with the omens read from it and the events that answered them, was already set down at length in the Book of Han's treatise on the subject.

sentences.zh: 故泰山太守應劭、給事中董巴、散騎常侍譙周並撰建武以來災異。

translations.literal: Therefore Ying Shao, prefect of Taishan, Dong Ba, palace attendant, and Qiao Zhou, regular attendant-in-ordinary of the scattered cavalry, together compiled prodigies and anomalies since the Jianwu era.
translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao, who had governed Taishan, the palace attendant Dong Ba, and Qiao Zhou, a regular attendant-in-ordinary of the scattered cavalry, each compiled records of portents and disasters from the opening of the Jianwu reign onward.

sentences.zh: 今合而論之，以續《前志》云。

translations.literal: Now combining and discussing them, so as to continue the former treatise.
translations.idiomatic: Here those materials are brought together and discussed in one place, extending the earlier treatise.

sentences.zh: 《五行傳》曰：「田獵不宿，飲食不享，出入不節，奪民農時，及有姦謀，則木不曲直。

translations.literal: The Treatise on the Five Elements says: "If one hunts without resting between outings, if one eats and drinks without offering sacrifice, if comings and goings lack moderation, if the people's farming seasons are seized from them, and if there are treacherous plots, then wood will not bend and straighten as it should."
translations.idiomatic: The Treatise on the Five Elements declares: "When the ruler hunts without pause, feasts without making the proper offerings, comes and goes without measure, robs the people of their seasons for tillage, and harbors secret treachery, the virtue associated with wood fails—wood no longer 'bends and straightens' as it ought."

sentences.zh: 」謂木失其性而爲災也。

translations.literal: " This means that wood loses its nature and becomes a disaster.
translations.idiomatic: That is to say, the nature of wood is corrupted and disaster follows.

sentences.zh: 又曰：「貌之不恭，是謂不肅。

translations.literal: It also says: "When there is lack of dignity in outward demeanor, this is called lack of solemnity."
translations.idiomatic: It continues: "When bearing is irreverent, that is termed a failure of awe-inspiring demeanor."

sentences.zh: 厥咎狂，厥罰恒雨，厥極惡。

translations.literal: Its fault is madness; its punishment is constant rain; its extreme is wickedness.
translations.idiomatic: The blame falls on frenzy; the chastisement is unrelenting rain; the worst outcome is thoroughgoing evil.

sentences.zh: 時則有服妖，時則有龜孽，時則有雞禍，時則有下體生上之痾，時則有青眚、青祥，惟金沴木。

translations.literal: Then there are clothing prodigies, then tortoise prodigies, then chicken disasters, then illness of the lower body appearing on the upper, then green calamities and green auspices—only metal injures wood.
translations.idiomatic: In such times appear freaks of dress, omens involving turtles, calamities among fowl, ailments that afflict the lower body yet show on the upper, bluish-green spectral visitations and greenish good-luck prodigies—metal, in the cycle of qi, is said to harm wood.

sentences.zh: 」說云：氣之相傷謂之沴。

translations.literal: " The explanation states: mutual injury among qi is called li (injurious interference).
translations.idiomatic: Commentary explains that when one phase of qi wounds another, that interaction is called li—injurious encroachment.

sentences.zh: 建武元年，赤眉賊率樊崇、逢安等共立劉盆子爲天子。

translations.literal: In the first year of Jianwu, the Red Eyebrow bandits, led by Fan Chong, Feng An, and others, together set up Liu Penzi as Son of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: In Jianwu's first year the Red Eyebrows, under Fan Chong and Feng An, enthroned the boy Liu Penzi as emperor.

sentences.zh: 然崇等視之如小兒，百事自由，初不恤錄也。

translations.literal: Yet Chong and the others treated him like a small child; in a hundred affairs he had freedom, and at first they did not care to restrain or supervise him.
translations.idiomatic: They treated him as a puppet, letting him have his way in trifles while never truly minding what he did.

sentences.zh: 後正旦至，君臣欲共饗，既坐，酒食未下，羣臣更起，亂不可整。

translations.literal: Later when New Year's Day arrived, ruler and ministers wished to feast together; they had already taken their seats, but before wine and food were served, the host of ministers rose one after another, and the disorder could not be set right.
translations.idiomatic: At the New Year banquet they had barely sat down when, before a cup was poured, the courtiers were on their feet again in such confusion that no one could restore order.

sentences.zh: 時，大司農楊音案劒怒曰：「小兒戲尚不如此！

translations.literal: At that time Grand Minister of Agriculture Yang Yin, grasping his sword in anger, said: "Even children's play is not like this!"
translations.idiomatic: Yang Yin, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, gripped his sword and swore that not even a nursery game would sink so low.

sentences.zh: 」其後遂破壞，崇、安等皆誅死。

translations.literal: " Afterward it was destroyed and broken up; Chong, An, and the others were all executed.
translations.idiomatic: The regime soon fell apart, and Fan Chong, Feng An, and their fellows were put to death.

sentences.zh: 唯音爲關内侯，以壽終。

translations.literal: Only Yin became marquis within the passes and ended his life by natural death.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Yin alone was ennobled as a marquis within the passes and died in bed of old age.

sentences.zh: 光武崩，山陽王荆哭不哀，作飛書與東海王，勸使作亂。

translations.literal: When Guangwu died, the Prince of Shanyang, Liu Jing, wept without grief; he composed a flying letter to the Prince of Donghai, urging him to rise in rebellion.
translations.idiomatic: After Guangwu's death Prince Jing of Shanyang showed so little sorrow at the bier that he was suspected at once; he then sent a secret letter to the Prince of Donghai, goading him into revolt.

sentences.zh: 明帝以荆同母弟，太后在，故隱之。

translations.literal: Mingdi, because Jing was his younger brother by the same mother and the empress dowager was still alive, therefore concealed the matter.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming hushed the affair out of respect for his mother the dowager, for Jing was his full brother.

sentences.zh: 後徙王廣陵，荆遂坐復謀反自殺也。

translations.literal: Later he was removed and made king of Guangling; Jing then sat guilty of again plotting rebellion and committed suicide.
translations.idiomatic: Later, when Jing was transferred to the kingdom of Guangling, he was caught plotting rebellion a second time and took his own life.

sentences.zh: 章帝時，竇皇后兄憲以皇后甚幸於上，故人人莫不畏憲。

translations.literal: In Zhangdi's time, Dou Xian, elder brother of Empress Dou, because the empress was greatly favored by the sovereign, therefore there was no one who did not fear Xian.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Zhang, Dou Xian—the empress's brother—terrified the whole court because his sister held the emperor's complete favor.

sentences.zh: 憲於是強請奪沁水長公主田，公主畏憲，與之，憲乃賤顧之。

translations.literal: Xian thereupon forcibly requested to seize the fields of the senior princess of Qinshui; the princess feared Xian and gave them to him; Xian then looked back on her with contempt.
translations.idiomatic: He bullied the senior Princess of Qinshui into surrendering her estate; once she yielded out of fear, he treated her with open contempt.

sentences.zh: 後上幸公主田，覺之，問憲，憲又上言借之。

translations.literal: Later when the sovereign visited the princess's fields, he perceived it; he questioned Xian, and Xian again submitted a memorial saying he had borrowed them.
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor later rode over those same fields and learned the truth, he confronted Dou Xian, who brazenly claimed he had only borrowed the land.

sentences.zh: 上以后故，但譴敕之，不治其罪。

translations.literal: The sovereign, because of the empress, only rebuked and admonished him and did not punish his crime.
translations.idiomatic: For the empress's sake the emperor limited himself to a stern reprimand and brought no charges.

sentences.zh: 後章帝崩，竇太后攝政，憲秉機密，忠直之臣與憲忤者，憲多害之，其後憲兄弟遂皆被誅。

translations.literal: Later when Zhangdi died, Empress Dowager Dou held the government; Xian grasped secret affairs; of the loyal and upright ministers who opposed Xian, Xian for the most part harmed them; afterward Xian and his brothers were all executed.
translations.idiomatic: After Zhangdi's death the Dou empress dowager ruled as regent while Dou Xian monopolized confidential business; anyone who stood up to him tended to disappear, until at last the whole Dou clan was wiped out.

sentences.zh: 桓帝時，梁冀秉政，兄弟貴盛自恣，好驅馳過度，至於歸家，猶馳驅入門。

translations.literal: In Huandi's time, Liang Ji held power; his brothers were noble and flourishing and gave themselves free rein; they loved to gallop to excess, so that even when returning home they still galloped through the gate.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Huan, Liang Ji dominated the government; his brothers were swaggering magnates who raced their chariots past all decency and would thunder through their own gates at a gallop.

sentences.zh: 百姓號之曰「梁氏滅門驅馳」，後遂誅滅。

translations.literal: The common people called it "the Liang clan's gallop to extermination of the whole house"; afterward they were indeed executed and destroyed.
translations.idiomatic: People took to calling their racing "the Liangs' headlong ride to clan extinction"—and in the end the prophecy was fulfilled to the letter.

sentences.zh: 和帝永元十年、十三年、十四年、十五年，皆淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In Emperor He's Yongyuan reign, the tenth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth years, in all cases excessive rain harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: Four separate years of Emperor He's Yongyuan era—10, 13, 14, and 15—brought such relentless rain that the harvests rotted in the fields.

sentences.zh: 安帝元年、四年秋，郡國十淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In Emperor An's first and fourth years, in autumn, ten commanderies and kingdoms had excessive rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: In the first and fourth years of Emperor An's reign, autumn storms ruined crops across ten provinces.

sentences.zh: 永寧元年，郡國三十三淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yongning, thirty-three commanderies and kingdoms had excessive rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: The first year of Yongning saw thirty-three commanderies and kingdoms deluged until the grain failed.

sentences.zh: 建光元年，京都及郡國二十九淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In the first year of Jianguang, the capital region and twenty-nine commanderies and kingdoms had excessive rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: Jianguang's first year brought the same affliction to the capital and twenty-nine other jurisdictions.

sentences.zh: 是時羌反久未平，百姓屯戍，不解愁苦。

translations.literal: At this time the Qiang rebellion had long not been pacified; the common people were garrisoned on campaign and could not be relieved of sorrow and bitterness.
translations.idiomatic: The Qiang revolt still raged, and the people—stuck in endless garrison duty—had no respite from misery.

sentences.zh: 延光元年，郡國二十七淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yanguang, twenty-seven commanderies and kingdoms had excessive rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: Yanguang's first year added twenty-seven more regions where the rains spoiled the harvest.

sentences.zh: 二年，郡國五連雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In the second year, five commanderies and kingdoms had continuous rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: The following year five commanderies suffered week after week of rain and lost their crops.

sentences.zh: 順帝永建四年，司隸、荆、豫、兗、冀部淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In Emperor Shun's fourth year of Yongjian, the Metropolitan Province and the Jing, Yu, Yan, and Ji regions had excessive rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth year of Yongjian under Emperor Shun, the capital inspectorate and the Jing, Yu, Yan, and Ji macro-regions were drowned by unseasonable rains.

sentences.zh: 六年，冀州淫雨傷稼。

translations.literal: In the sixth year, Ji Province had excessive rain that harmed the crops.
translations.idiomatic: Two years later Ji Province alone was battered by the same scourge.

sentences.zh: 桓帝延熹二年夏，霖雨五十餘日。

translations.literal: In Emperor Huan's second year of Yanxi, summer, there was soaking rain for more than fifty days.
translations.idiomatic: In the second summer of Emperor Huan's Yanxi era the skies opened for fifty-odd days of steady downpour.

sentences.zh: 是時，大將軍梁冀秉政，謀害上所幸鄧貴人母宣，冀又擅殺議郎邴尊。

translations.literal: At this time the great general Liang Ji held power; he plotted to harm Xuan, mother of the honored Lady Deng whom the sovereign favored; Ji also on his own authority killed Gentleman-advisor Bing Zun.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji was then dictator at court: he schemed against Lady Deng's mother Xuan, whom the emperor cherished, and he murdered the advisor Bing Zun without trial.

sentences.zh: 上欲誅冀，懼其持權日久，威勢強盛，恐有逆命，害及吏民，密與近臣中常侍單超等圖其方畧。

translations.literal: The sovereign wished to execute Ji, but feared that because he had held power a long time his awesomeness and strength were great, and dreaded that there might be defiance of orders, harm reaching officials and people; he secretly with close ministers, palace attendant Shan Chao and others, plotted the strategy.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor meant to destroy Liang Ji yet dreaded the general's entrenched might; he feared a violent refusal that would cost officials and commoners their lives, so he took Shan Chao and other trusted eunuchs into his confidence and worked out a plan in secret.

sentences.zh: 其年八月，冀卒伏罪誅滅。

translations.literal: That year in the eighth month, Ji finally submitted to guilt and was executed and exterminated.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth month of that same year Liang Ji was convicted and the entire faction extirpated.

sentences.zh: 中平六年夏，霖雨八十餘日。

translations.literal: In the sixth year of Zhongping, summer, there was soaking rain for more than eighty days.
translations.idiomatic: The sixth year of Zhongping brought eighty-some days of unbroken summer rain.

sentences.zh: 是時，靈帝新棄羣臣，大行尚在梓宫，大將軍何進與佐軍校尉袁紹等共謀欲誅廢中官。

translations.literal: At this time Lingdi had newly abandoned the host of ministers; the grand procession was still in the catalpa coffin; the great general He Jin with assistant army commandant Yuan Shao and others together plotted wishing to execute and abolish the inner court eunuchs.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling had just died; his bier still stood in the palace when He Jin the general-in-chief and Yuan Shao, an assistant commandant of the army, conspired to slaughter the eunuchs and strip them of office.

sentences.zh: 下文陵畢，中常侍張讓等共殺進，兵戰京都，死者數千。

translations.literal: After the burial rites at Wenling were completed, palace attendants Zhang Rang and others together killed Jin; soldiers fought in the capital region; those who died were several thousand.
translations.idiomatic: Once Emperor Ling had been interred at Wenling, Zhang Rang and his fellow eunuchs cut down He Jin; Luoyang erupted in street fighting and thousands died.

sentences.zh: 更始諸將軍過雒陽者數十辈，皆帻而衣婦人衣繡擁蕭。

translations.literal: The various generals of Gengshi who passed through Luoyang numbered several tens of parties; all wore headcloths and dressed in women's embroidered clothing with piled-up sedge.
translations.idiomatic: Dozens of Gengshi-era generals marched through Luoyang wearing turbans over women's embroidered gowns, their hair dressed in elaborate coils.

sentences.zh: 時，智者見之，以爲服之不中，身之災也，乃奔入邊郡避之。

translations.literal: At that time, when wise men saw it, they considered that clothing not hitting the mark was a disaster for the person; they then fled into border commanderies to avoid it.
translations.idiomatic: Thoughtful observers took this perversion of dress for a personal ill omen and fled to the frontier for safety.

sentences.zh: 是服妖也。

translations.literal: This was a clothing prodigy.
translations.idiomatic: This was reckoned a "clothing prodigy" in the sense of the omen texts.

sentences.zh: 其後更始遂爲赤眉所殺。

translations.literal: Afterward Gengshi was then killed by the Red Eyebrows.
translations.idiomatic: Gengshi soon fell to the Red Eyebrows and lost his life.

sentences.zh: 桓帝元嘉中，京都婦女作愁眉、啼粧、堕馬髻、折要步、齲齒笑。

translations.literal: In Huandi's Yuanjia era, capital women made sorrowful brows, weeping makeup, fallen-horse chignons, broken-waist gait, and decayed-tooth smiles.
translations.idiomatic: During Emperor Huan's Yuanjia years the women of Luoyang took up "grieving" brows, tear-stained cosmetics, side-swept chignons styled like a tumble from a horse, a mincing walk that snapped at the waist, and smiles that bared teeth as if in pain.

sentences.zh: 所謂愁眉者，細而曲折。

translations.literal: What is called sorrowful brows means fine and tortuous.
translations.idiomatic: The "sorrowful" brow was plucked thin and drawn in nervous curves.

sentences.zh: 啼粧者，薄拭目下，若啼處。

translations.literal: Weeping makeup means lightly wiping beneath the eyes as if a place where one weeps.
translations.idiomatic: The "weeping" face was rouged only under the eyes, as though fresh from tears.

sentences.zh: 堕馬髻者，作一邊。

translations.literal: Fallen-horse chignon means made to one side.
translations.idiomatic: The "fallen-from-a-horse" coiffure swept all the hair to one side.

sentences.zh: 折要步者，足不在體下。

translations.literal: Broken-waist gait means the feet are not beneath the body.
translations.idiomatic: The "broken waist" walk kept the feet from falling straight under the torso—an exaggerated sway.

sentences.zh: 齲齒笑者，若齒痛，樂不欣欣。

translations.literal: Decay-tooth smile means as if the teeth hurt; joy is not bright and glad.
translations.idiomatic: The "rotting-tooth" smile looked like a wince of dental pain—mirth without merriment.

sentences.zh: 始自大將軍梁冀家所爲，京都歙然，諸夏皆放效。

translations.literal: It began as what was done in the household of the great general Liang Ji; the capital sucked in its breath; all the Xia lands imitated it.
translations.idiomatic: The fashion started in General Liang Ji's mansion, swept the capital overnight, and was copied through the heartland.

sentences.zh: 此近服妖也。

translations.literal: This was near to a clothing prodigy.
translations.idiomatic: This was reckoned a near cousin to the omen of freakish dress.

sentences.zh: 梁冀二世上將，婚媾王室，大作威福，將危社稷。

translations.literal: Liang Ji for two generations was chief general; he married into the royal house and greatly made awesomeness and blessings, about to endanger the altars of soil and grain.
translations.idiomatic: For two generations the Liangs had held the supreme command, intermarried with the imperial clan, thrown their weight about, and brought the dynasty to the brink.

sentences.zh: 天誡若曰：「兵馬將往收捕，婦女憂愁，踧眉啼泣，吏卒掣頓，折其要脊，令髻傾邪，雖強語笑，无復氣味也。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning was as if saying: "When horses and foot-soldiers are about to go to seize and capture, women are anxious and sorrowful, knitting their brows and weeping; clerks and soldiers drag and halt them, break their waist and spine, make their chignons lean awry; though they force speech and laughter, there is no more breath or flavor."
translations.idiomatic: Heaven seemed to warn: "Troops are coming to drag families away—women will weep and cringe, guards will wrench their backs and snap their spines, their hair will hang askew, and any laughter they manage will be hollow."

sentences.zh: 」到延熹二年，舉宗誅夷。

translations.literal: " When it reached the second year of Yanxi, the whole clan was executed and exterminated.
translations.idiomatic: In the second Yanxi year the entire Liang clan was extirpated.

sentences.zh: 延熹中，梁冀誅后，京都帻颜短耳長，短上長下。

translations.literal: In the Yanxi era, after Liang Ji was executed, in the capital the headcloth's face was short and the ears long, short above and long below.
translations.idiomatic: After Liang Ji's fall, during the Yanxi years, Luoyang took to turbans cut short across the crown with long flaps at the ears—the upper line abrupt, the lower line drawn out.

sentences.zh: 時中常侍單超、左悺、徐璜、具瑗、唐衡在帝左右，縱其姦慝。

translations.literal: At that time palace attendants Shan Chao, Zuo Guan, Xu Huang, Ju Yuan, and Tang Heng were at the emperor's side and gave free rein to their treacherous wickedness.
translations.idiomatic: Shan Chao, Zuo Guan, Xu Huang, Ju Yuan, and Tang Heng—the eunuch quintet at the emperor's elbow—ran wild with corruption.

sentences.zh: 海内愠曰：一將軍死，五將軍出。

translations.literal: Within the seas people resentfully said: one general died, five generals came forth.
translations.idiomatic: A bitter proverb ran through the realm: "One general-in-chief falls—five spring up to replace him."

sentences.zh: 家有數侯，子弟列布州郡，宾客杂袭腾翥，上短下長，與梁冀同占。

translations.literal: Families had several marquises; sons and younger brothers were spread through provinces and commanderies; guests and retainers mixed and thronged, soaring upward; short above and long below, with the same divination as Liang Ji.
translations.idiomatic: Each household boasted multiple marquises, their sons planted in every province, their clients flocking like birds on the wing; the fashion—short above, long below—mirrored the omen once read from Liang Ji's excess.

sentences.zh: 到其八年，桓帝因日蚀之變，乃拜故司徒韩寅爲司隸校尉，以次誅鉏，京都正清。

translations.literal: When it reached its eighth year, Huandi because of the change of a solar eclipse then appointed former minister of education Han Yin as metropolitan commandant, and in order executed and extirpated them; the capital region was set right and cleared.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth year of that reign Emperor Huan seized on a solar eclipse as his cue, named the former minister Han Yin metropolitan commandant, and purged the eunuch faction step by step until Luoyang was clean again.

sentences.zh: 延熹中，京都長者皆著木屐；

translations.literal: In the Yanxi era, elders of the capital all wore wooden clogs;
translations.idiomatic: During Yanxi the respectable men of Luoyang went about in wooden clogs;

sentences.zh: 婦女始嫁，至作漆画五采爲系。

translations.literal: women beginning marriage even made lacquer-painted five-colors as ties.
translations.idiomatic: brides began tying their hair with lacquered ribbons painted in five colors.

sentences.zh: 此服妖也。

translations.literal: This was a clothing prodigy.
translations.idiomatic: Another sign in the category of freakish dress.

sentences.zh: 到九年，党事始发，傳黄門北寺，临時惶惑，不能信天任命，多有逃走不就考者，九族拘繫，及所過歷，長少婦女皆被桎梏，應木屐之象也。

translations.literal: When it reached the ninth year, the faction affair first broke out; it was transmitted to the Northern Office of the Yellow Gates; facing the moment, people were anxious and confused, unable to trust Heaven and accept fate; many there were who fled and did not submit to examination; nine kin were bound and tied; and wherever they passed, old and young women all wore fetters and cangues, corresponding to the image of wooden clogs.
translations.idiomatic: In the ninth year the great proscription began; suspects were hustled into the eunuchs' North Prison. Panic spread—men no longer trusted providence, many bolted rather than face interrogation, whole clans were shackled, and wherever the dragnet reached, women young and old were marched off in cangues and leg-irons, the very picture the wooden clogs had foretold.

sentences.zh: 靈帝建寧中，京都長者皆以苇方笥爲粧具，下士尽然。

translations.literal: In Lingdi's Jianning era, elders of the capital all used reed square cases as toilet articles; lower gentlemen all did likewise.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Ling, during Jianning, the capital's leading families kept their cosmetics in square reed boxes—and soon every petty clerk aped the style.

sentences.zh: 時有識者窃言：苇方笥，郡國讞箧也；

translations.literal: At that time someone with insight secretly said: reed square cases are the appeal boxes of commanderies and kingdoms;
translations.idiomatic: Wits whispered that those reed cases were the very "appeal caskets" in which provinces filed criminal memorials;

sentences.zh: 今珍用之，此天下人皆當有罪讞於理官也。

translations.literal: now they are treasured and used; this means everyone under Heaven ought to have crimes appealed to the judge officials.
translations.idiomatic: to prize them for rouge and powder meant the whole empire would soon stand convicted before the law.

sentences.zh: 到光和三年癸丑赦令詔書，吏民依黨禁錮者赦除之，有不見文，他以類比疑者谳。

translations.literal: When it reached the third year of Guanghe, guichou, the amnesty-order edict: officials and people who according to the faction proscription had been proscribed were pardoned and removed; where the text was not seen, other doubtful cases by analogy were appealed for decision.
translations.idiomatic: In the third year of Guanghe, on the guichou day, an edict of general amnesty lifted the faction ban—where the wording was unclear, doubtful cases were sent up for the court to decide by analogy.

sentences.zh: 於是諸有黨郡皆讞廷尉，人名悉入方笥中。

translations.literal: Thereupon all commanderies that had faction cases all appealed to the commandant of justice; people's names all went into square cases.
translations.idiomatic: Every county with a "faction" list forwarded its dossiers to the commandant of justice, and the accused were filed away—names and all—in those square reed boxes.

sentences.zh: 靈帝好胡服、胡帳、胡牀、胡坐、胡飯、胡空侯、胡笛、胡舞，京都貴戚皆竞爲之。

translations.literal: Lingdi loved Hu clothing, Hu tents, Hu couches, Hu sitting, Hu food, Hu konghou, Hu flutes, Hu dances; capital nobles and kin all vied to do it.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling doted on frontier dress, frontier tents, folding chairs, cross-legged sitting, frontier dishes, barbarian lutes and pipes, and barbarian dance—and the great families of Luoyang rushed to outdo one another.

sentences.zh: 此服妖也。

translations.literal: This was a clothing prodigy.
translations.idiomatic: Another omen-class freak of dress.

sentences.zh: 其後董卓多擁胡兵，填塞街衢，虏掠宫掖，发掘園陵。

translations.literal: Afterward Dong Zhuo for the most part gathered Hu troops, filled and blocked streets and lanes, plundered the palace apartments, and dug up park tombs.
translations.idiomatic: Then Dong Zhuo flooded the capital with steppe troops, choked the avenues, looted the inner palaces, and broke open imperial tombs.

sentences.zh: 靈帝於宫中西園駕四白驢，躬自操轡，驅馳周旋，以爲大樂。

translations.literal: Lingdi in the palace at the Western Garden drove four white donkeys, personally grasped the reins, galloped round and about, and took it as great pleasure.
translations.idiomatic: In the Western Garden inside the palace Emperor Ling hitched four white donkeys, seized the reins himself, and raced in circles for sport.

sentences.zh: 於是公卿貴戚转相放效，至乘辎軿以爲騎從，互相侵奪，贾與馬齊。

translations.literal: Thereupon dukes and ministers and noble kin in turn imitated one another, to the point of riding covered wagons as mounted attendants, mutually encroaching and seizing; the price matched that of horses.
translations.idiomatic: High ministers and imperial in-laws copied the fad until they used light wagons as outriders in their escorts, jostling one another on the road until a donkey cost as much as a horse.

sentences.zh: 案《易》曰：「時乘六龍以御天。

translations.literal: Examining the Changes, it says: "In due season mount the six dragons to drive Heaven."
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Changes says of the sage ruler that he "rides the six dragons to traverse Heaven."

sentences.zh: 」行天者莫若龍，行地者莫若馬。

translations.literal: " For what travels Heaven nothing is like the dragon; for what travels Earth nothing is like the horse.
translations.idiomatic: Nothing matches the dragon for motion above, nothing the horse for motion below.

sentences.zh: 《詩》云：「四牡騤騤，載是常服。

translations.literal: The Odes says: "The four stallions are stately; they bear the regular harness."
translations.idiomatic: The Classic of Poetry praises the team: "Four tall stallions in full battle harness."

sentences.zh: 」「檀車煌煌，四牡彭彭。

translations.literal: " "The sandalwood carriage gleams; the four stallions are vigorous."
translations.idiomatic: Elsewhere it sings of "the gleaming sandalwood car and four powerful steeds."

sentences.zh: 」夫驢乃服重致遠，上下山谷，野人之所用耳，何有帝王君子而驂服之乎！

translations.literal: " Now the donkey is for bearing heavy loads and going far, ascending and descending mountains and valleys—what the wild people use; how can there be emperors and kings and gentlemen who pair and drive them!
translations.idiomatic: The donkey is a beast of burden for hill folk—how could Son of Heaven or a gentleman take it for a chariot team!

sentences.zh: 迟鈍之畜，而今貴之。

translations.literal: A slow and dull animal, yet now it is honored.
translations.idiomatic: A dull, plodding creature—yet the court now prizes it.

sentences.zh: 天意若曰：國且大亂，賢愚倒植，凡執政者皆如驢也。

translations.literal: Heaven's intent was as if saying: the state is about to be greatly disordered; worthy and foolish are inverted; all who hold power are like donkeys.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven's message read: "The realm will soon convulse; wise and foolish will trade places, and every man at the helm will be a donkey."

sentences.zh: 其後董卓陵虐王室，多援邊人以充本朝，胡夷異种，跨蹈中國。

translations.literal: Afterward Dong Zhuo cruelly abused the royal house; he largely drew in border people to fill this court; Hu and Yi of alien stocks trampled the central states.
translations.idiomatic: Dong Zhuo then rode roughshod over the dynasty, drafting frontier peoples into the capital until foreign tribes overran the heartland.

sentences.zh: 熹平中，省内冠狗带綬，以爲笑樂。

translations.literal: In the Xiping era, within the palace they capped dogs and belted seals of office, taking it as laughter and pleasure.
translations.idiomatic: During Xiping the inner palace staged mock investitures—dogs in official caps and ribboned seals—for amusement.

sentences.zh: 有一狗突出，走入司徒府門，或見之者，莫不惊怪。

translations.literal: There was one dog that burst out and ran into the gate of the minister of education's office; those who saw it were all startled and wondered.
translations.idiomatic: One dog broke loose and dashed into the gate of the Minister of Education—every witness was struck with dread.

sentences.zh: 京房《易傳》曰：「君不正，臣欲篡，厥妖狗冠出。

translations.literal: Jing Fang's Commentary on the Changes says: "When the lord is not correct, ministers wish to usurp; its prodigy is a capped dog appearing."
translations.idiomatic: Jing Fang's treatise warns: "When the ruler strays from the Way and ministers plot usurpation, Heaven sends the prodigy of a dog in an official's cap."

sentences.zh: 」后靈帝寵用便嬖子弟，永樂宾客、鸿都羣小，傳相汲引，公卿牧守，比肩是也。

translations.literal: " Later Lingdi favored and employed the sons and younger brothers of his intimates, guests of Yongle, the petty crowd of Hongdu; they transmitted and drew one another up; dukes, ministers, shepherds, and guards—shoulder to shoulder were such.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling went on to shower favor on his minions' sons, the hangers-on at Yongle, the riffraff of the Hongdu Academy—men who pulled one another up until every minister and provincial governor seemed cut from the same cloth.

sentences.zh: 又遣御史於西邸卖官，關内侯顧五百萬者，赐與金紫；

translations.literal: He also sent censors to the Western Lodge to sell offices; for one who looked to a marquis within the passes at five million, he was granted gold and purple;
translations.idiomatic: He set up a market for ranks at the Western Lodge: five million cash bought a marquisate within the passes and the gold seal with purple ribbon;

sentences.zh: 詣闕上書占令長，随县好醜，豐約有賈。

translations.literal: Those who went to the palace gate and submitted memorials to secure magistrates, following whether the county was good or ugly, had abundance or restraint with a price.
translations.idiomatic: Anyone could walk to the palace gate, bid for a magistracy, and pay a sliding scale—fat fees for rich counties, lean ones for poor.

sentences.zh: 強者貪如豺虎，弱者畧不類物，實狗而冠者也。

translations.literal: The strong were greedy as jackals and tigers; the weak were in outline not like creatures—truly dogs wearing caps.
translations.idiomatic: The bold ones devoured like wolves; the timid ones scarcely looked human—they were dogs in caps, nothing more.

sentences.zh: 司徒，古之丞相，壹统國政。

translations.literal: The minister of education is the ancient chancellor; he alone unifies state government.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education was once the chancellor—the officer who unified the administration of the realm.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰：宰相多非其人，尸祿素餐，莫能据正持重，阿意曲從。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning was as if saying: the ministers are mostly not the right men; they hold salary with empty white eating; none can grasp what is correct and hold weight; they flatter intent and bend in compliance.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven seemed to warn: "Too many chief ministers are the wrong men—drawing pay for empty seats, unable to stand firm, always trimming to the ruler's whim."

sentences.zh: 今在位者皆如狗也，故狗走入其門。

translations.literal: Now those in office are all like dogs; therefore the dog ran into their gate.
translations.idiomatic: The men in power were hounds in caps—which is why Heaven sent a dog through the minister's gate.

sentences.zh: 靈帝數游戲於西園中，令後宫采女爲客舍主人，身爲商賈服。

translations.literal: Lingdi repeatedly played games in the Western Garden; he ordered rear-palace selected women to be innkeepers; he himself wore merchant-trader clothing.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling often staged bawdy play in the Western Garden, dressing palace ladies as innkeepers while he himself put on the garb of a peddler.

sentences.zh: 行至舍，采女下酒食，因共飲食以爲戲樂。

translations.literal: When he walked and reached the inn, the selected women set out wine and food; thereupon they together drank and ate, taking it as playful pleasure.
translations.idiomatic: He would "arrive" at the mock inn; the women served wine and food, and all feasted together for sport.

sentences.zh: 此服妖也。

translations.literal: This was a clothing prodigy.
translations.idiomatic: Another omen in the category of perverted dress.

sentences.zh: 其後天下大亂。

translations.literal: Afterward all under Heaven was greatly disordered.
translations.idiomatic: The empire then slid into chaos.

sentences.zh: 獻帝建安中，男子之衣，好爲長躬而下甚短，女子好爲長裙而上甚短。

translations.literal: In Xiandi's Jian'an era, men's clothing favored making the upper body long while below was very short; women favored making long skirts while above was very short.
translations.idiomatic: In the Jian'an years of Emperor Xian, men wore jackets that hung long on the torso but ended abruptly at the waist, while women favored long skirts paired with bodices cut scandalously short.

sentences.zh: 時益州從事莫嗣以爲服妖，是陽无下而陰无上也，天下未欲平也。

translations.literal: At the time the Yizhou clerk Mo Si took it to be a clothing prodigy: this was yang having nothing below and yin having nothing above; all under Heaven did not yet desire peace.
translations.idiomatic: Mo Si, an aide in Yi Province, read the new fashions as an ill omen: the masculine had lost its footing, the feminine its summit—the realm was not ready to rest.

sentences.zh: 后還，遂大亂。

translations.literal: Later he returned, and thereupon there was great disorder.
translations.idiomatic: He was proved right when the emperor came back from exile and the world slid into chaos.

sentences.zh: 桓帝永興二年四月丙午，光祿勋吏舍壁下夜有青氣，視之，得玉鈎、玦各一。

translations.literal: In Huandi's second year of Yongxing, fourth month, day bingwu, beneath the wall of the clerks' quarters of the chamberlain for the palace revenues, at night there was greenish vapor; looking at it, they obtained one jade hook and one jade ring apiece.
translations.idiomatic: On a bingwu day in the fourth month of Yongxing 2, a greenish glow appeared at night under the eunuch finance office; when clerks dug there they found a carved jade belt hook and a broken ring.

sentences.zh: 鈎長七寸二分，玦周五寸四分，身中皆雕鏤。

translations.literal: The hook was seven cun and two fen in length; the ring's circumference was five cun and four fen; their bodies were all carved openwork.
translations.idiomatic: The hook measured seven cun two fen; the ring's girth was five cun four fen; both pieces were richly engraved.

sentences.zh: 此青祥也，玉，金類也。

translations.literal: This was a green auspice; jade is of the class of metal.
translations.idiomatic: Green jade prodigies belong to the wood-metal nexus—jade itself counts as a metal-like substance in the scheme.

sentences.zh: 七寸二分，商數也。

translations.literal: Seven cun two fen is the shang pitch number.
translations.idiomatic: Seven cun two fen matches the "shang" tone in the pitch-pipe numerology.

sentences.zh: 五寸四分，徵數也。

translations.literal: Five cun four fen is the zhi pitch number.
translations.idiomatic: Five cun four fen answers to the "zhi" pipe.

sentences.zh: 商爲臣，徵爲事，盖爲人臣引决事者不肅，將有禍也。

translations.literal: Shang stands for ministers, zhi for affairs: it means that ministers who lead in deciding affairs are not solemn; there will be disaster.
translations.idiomatic: Because "shang" codes for ministers and "zhi" for public business, the omen pointed to high officials who shaped policy without gravity—disaster would follow.

sentences.zh: 是時梁冀秉政專恣，后四岁，梁氏誅滅也。

translations.literal: At that time Liang Ji held power and was wantonly autocratic; after four years the Liang clan was executed and destroyed.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji was then absolute master of the court; four years later his whole clan was extirpated.

sentences.zh: 延熹五年，太学門无故自壞。

translations.literal: In the fifth year of Yanxi, the gate of the Imperial Academy for no reason collapsed of itself.
translations.idiomatic: In Yanxi 5 the main gate of the Imperial Academy fell in though no one had touched it.

sentences.zh: 襄楷以爲太学前疑所居，其門自壞，文德將喪，教化廢也。

translations.literal: Xiang Kai considered that the Imperial Academy was where the former doubtful resided; its gate collapsed of itself: civil virtue was about to be lost, instruction and transformation were abandoned.
translations.idiomatic: Xiang Kai argued that the academy had housed the ancient "doubtful" star; when its gate gave way of its own accord, it foretold the collapse of moral culture and the abandonment of education.

sentences.zh: 是後天下遂至喪亂。

translations.literal: After this all under Heaven thereupon reached ruin and disorder.
translations.idiomatic: The empire soon sank into anarchy.

sentences.zh: 永康元年十月壬戌，南宫平城門内屋自壞。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yongkang, tenth month, day renxu, buildings inside the Pingcheng Gate of the Southern Palace collapsed of themselves.
translations.idiomatic: On a renxu day in the tenth month of Yongkang 1, structures inside Luoyang's Pingcheng Gate in the Southern Palace fell without warning.

sentences.zh: 金沴木，木動也。

translations.literal: Metal injures wood; wood moved.
translations.idiomatic: Metal was encroaching on wood—the element of timber shook.

sentences.zh: 其十二月，宫車晏駕。

translations.literal: That twelfth month, the palace carriage delayed its departure (the emperor died).
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth month the emperor died—the euphemism "the palace carriage tarried."

sentences.zh: 三年二月，公府驻駕庑自壞，南北三十餘間。

translations.literal: In the third year, second month, the portico where the public offices halted the imperial carriage collapsed of itself, more than thirty bays north and south.
translations.idiomatic: In the third year, second month, the colonnade where ministers waited on the imperial progress collapsed—over thirty bays along the north-south range.

sentences.zh: 中平一年二月癸亥，廣陽城門外上屋自壞也。

translations.literal: In the first year of Zhongping, second month, day guihai, the upper buildings outside the Guangyang city gate collapsed of themselves.
translations.idiomatic: On a guihai day in the second month of Zhongping 1, the upper structures outside Luoyang's Guangyang Gate crumbled on their own.

sentences.zh: 獻帝初平二年三月，長安宣平城門外屋无故自壞。

translations.literal: In Xiandi's second year of Chuping, third month, buildings outside Chang'an's Xuanping city gate for no reason collapsed of themselves.
translations.idiomatic: In the third month of Chuping 2, under Emperor Xian, the buildings outside Chang'an's Xuanping Gate fell in though no storm had struck.

sentences.zh: 至三年夏，司徒王允使中郎將吕布殺太师董卓，夷三族。

translations.literal: By the third year, summer, Minister of Education Wang Yun had leader of gentlemen cadets Lü Bu kill grand preceptor Dong Zhuo and exterminate three clans.
translations.idiomatic: In the summer of the third year Minister Wang Yun sent Lü Bu to cut down Dong Zhuo the grand preceptor and wipe out three generations of his kin.

sentences.zh: 《五行傳》曰：「好攻戰，轻百姓，饰城郭，侵邊境，則金不從革。

translations.literal: The Treatise on the Five Elements says: "If one loves attacking and warfare, treats the common people lightly, adorns city walls, and encroaches on the borderlands, then metal will not follow and transform."
translations.idiomatic: The Treatise on the Five Elements warns that when rulers delight in war, despise the people, gild their ramparts, and raid the frontiers, the virtue of metal fails—it no longer "yields and changes" as it should.

sentences.zh: 」謂金失其性而爲災也。

translations.literal: " This means that metal loses its nature and becomes a disaster.
translations.idiomatic: That is, the nature of metal is corrupted and calamity follows.

sentences.zh: 又曰：「言之不從，是謂不乂。

translations.literal: It also says: "When speech does not obey, this is called lack of order (bu yi)."
translations.idiomatic: It adds: "When counsel goes unheeded, that is termed a breakdown of good government."

sentences.zh: 厥咎僭，厥罰恒陽，厥極憂。

translations.literal: Its fault is usurpation; its punishment is constant yang (drought); its extreme is sorrow.
translations.idiomatic: The fault is overreaching; the scourge is relentless drought; the bitter end is widespread grief.

sentences.zh: 時則有詩妖，時則有介虫之孽，時則有犬禍，時則有口舌之痾，時則有白眚、白祥、惟木沴金。

translations.literal: Then there are song prodigies, then shelled-insect prodigies, then dog disasters, then illness of mouth and tongue, then white calamities and white auspices—only wood injures metal.
translations.idiomatic: Such ages bring rhymed portents, plagues among armored insects, canine omens, ailments of speech, pallid spectral blights—and in the cycle of qi, wood is said to harm metal.

sentences.zh: 」介虫，劉歆傳以爲毛虫。

translations.literal: " Shelled insects—in Liu Xin's transmission they are taken to be hairy creatures.
translations.idiomatic: Commentators following Liu Xin class the "shelled" pests with hairy vermin omens.

sentences.zh: 乂，治也。

translations.literal: Yi means to govern.
translations.idiomatic: Here yi means orderly rule.

sentences.zh: 安帝永初元年十一月，民讹言相惊，司隸、並、冀州民人流移。

translations.literal: In Emperor An's first year of Yongchu, eleventh month, the people with false words alarmed one another; the people of the Metropolitan Province, Bing, and Ji flowed away in migration.
translations.idiomatic: In the eleventh month of Yongchu 1 wild rumors threw the people into panic; refugees streamed from the capital region, Bing, and Ji.

sentences.zh: 時，鄧太皇專政。

translations.literal: At that time Empress Dowager Deng held sole power.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Dowager Deng was then regent in all but name.

sentences.zh: 婦人以順爲道，故《禮》「夫死從子」之命。

translations.literal: Women take compliance as their way; therefore the Rites have the command "when the husband dies, follow the son."
translations.idiomatic: A woman's virtue was submission; the canonical Rites therefore ordain that when her husband dies she obeys her son.

sentences.zh: 今專主事，此不從而僭也。

translations.literal: Now she solely presides over affairs; this is not obeying but usurping.
translations.idiomatic: To monopolize state business was neither "following" a man nor staying within a woman's sphere—it was usurpation.

sentences.zh: 世祖建武五年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Shizu's fifth year of Jianwu, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: A drought struck in the summer of Emperor Guangwu's fifth Jianwu year.

sentences.zh: 《京房傳》曰：「欲德不用，兹謂張，厥災荒，其旱陰雲不雨，變而赤，因四陰。

translations.literal: Jing Fang's Treatise says: "When desired virtue is not used, this is called stretching; its disaster is wasteland; its drought—yin clouds do not rain, they change and become red, following the four yin."
translations.idiomatic: Jing Fang lists omens of drought: when virtue is spurned, Heaven stretches the land into waste; clouds gather but yield no rain, then flush an ominous red as yin forces encroach.

sentences.zh: 眾出過時，兹謂廣，其旱不生。

translations.literal: When hosts go out beyond the season, this is called broadening; its drought—nothing grows.
translations.idiomatic: Armies kept in the field too long "spread" exhaustion; the fields then refuse every shoot.

sentences.zh: 上下皆蔽，兹謂隔，其旱天赤三月，時有雹殺飛禽。

translations.literal: When above and below are both obscured, this is called blocking; its drought—the sky is red three months; at times hail kills flying birds.
translations.idiomatic: When ruler and minister deceive each other, Heaven "blocks" the rain—the heavens burn red for months and hailstones cut down birds in flight.

sentences.zh: 上缘求妃，兹謂僭，其旱三月大温亡云。

translations.literal: When the sovereign on account seeks concubines, this is called usurpation; its drought—three months of great warmth without clouds.
translations.idiomatic: A ruler who chases women beyond measure commits usurpation against Heaven; the land then swelters for three cloudless months.

sentences.zh: 君高臺府，兹謂犯，陰侵陽，其旱萬物根死，有火災。

translations.literal: When the lord raises high terraces and mansions, this is called violation; yin encroaches on yang; its drought—the roots of the myriad things die; there are fire disasters.
translations.idiomatic: Towering palaces offend the balance of yin and yang; drought kills every root, and fires follow.

sentences.zh: 庶位逾節，兹謂僭，其旱泽物枯，爲火所傷。

translations.literal: When common offices exceed their measure, this is called usurpation; its drought—marsh things wither and are harmed by fire.
translations.idiomatic: When petty officials overstep their rank, usurpation dries the wetlands and scorches what should be moist.

sentences.zh: 」是時，天下僭逆者未尽誅，軍多過時。

translations.literal: " At this time those who had usurped and rebelled under Heaven had not all been executed; armies were for the most part beyond their season.
translations.idiomatic: Rebels still lived while imperial columns overstayed in the field—both sins on Jing Fang's list.

sentences.zh: 章帝章和二年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Zhangdi's second year of Zhanghe, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Drought gripped the summer of Zhanghe 2 under Emperor Zhang.

sentences.zh: 時，章帝崩后，竇太后兄弟用事奢僭。

translations.literal: At that time, after Zhangdi died, Empress Dowager Dou's brothers held power, extravagant and usurping.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Zhang had just died; the Dou brothers flaunted power for their sister the dowager, spending wildly beyond their station.

sentences.zh: 和帝永元六年秋，京都旱。

translations.literal: In Emperor He's sixth year of Yongyuan, autumn, the capital region had drought.
translations.idiomatic: Luoyang baked under drought in the autumn of Yongyuan 6.

sentences.zh: 時，雒陽有冤囚，和帝幸雒陽寺，錄囚徒，理冤囚，收令下獄抵罪。

translations.literal: At that time in Luoyang there were unjust prisoners; He visited the Luoyang jail, reviewed convicts, set right unjust prisoners, seized the magistrate and sent him down to prison to answer for his crime.
translations.idiomatic: A miscarriage of justice in Luoyang brought Emperor He in person to the city jail; he freed the innocent, jailed the magistrate, and laid the charge at his door.

sentences.zh: 行未還宫，澍雨降。

translations.literal: Before he had returned walking to the palace, soaking rain fell.
translations.idiomatic: He had not yet reached the palace when a soaking rain began to fall.

sentences.zh: 安帝永初六年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Emperor An's sixth year of Yongchu, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: The summer of Yongchu 6 brought drought under Emperor An.

sentences.zh: 七年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the seventh year, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Drought returned the following summer.

sentences.zh: 元初元年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yuanchu, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanchu's first summer was rainless.

sentences.zh: 二年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the second year, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: The next summer brought drought again.

sentences.zh: 六年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the sixth year, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Four years later another parched summer arrived.

sentences.zh: 順帝永建三年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Emperor Shun's third year of Yongjian, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shun's third Yongjian summer was a season of drought.

sentences.zh: 五年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the fifth year, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Two years later drought struck again.

sentences.zh: 陽嘉二年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the second year of Yangjia, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Yangjia 2 brought another rainless summer.

sentences.zh: 時，李固对策，以爲奢僭所致也。

translations.literal: At that time Li Gu in his examination answer considered that it was caused by extravagance and usurpation.
translations.idiomatic: Li Gu, answering the court's policy questions, blamed the skies on luxury and overreaching.

sentences.zh: 冲帝永熹元年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Emperor Chong's first year of Yongxi, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: The child-emperor Chong's sole summer reign year opened with drought.

sentences.zh: 時，冲帝幼崩，太尉李固勸太后兄梁冀立嗣帝，擇年長有德者，天下賴之，則功名不朽。

translations.literal: At that time Emperor Chong died young; Grand Commandant Li Gu urged the empress dowager's brother Liang Ji to establish an heir-emperor, choosing one advanced in years and possessed of virtue; if all under Heaven relied on him, then merit and fame would not perish.
translations.idiomatic: When the boy emperor died, Li Gu the grand commandant begged Liang Ji to choose a mature, virtuous heir so the realm might rally and their own names live on.

sentences.zh: 年幼未可知，如后不善，悔无所及。

translations.literal: If young, one cannot know; if afterward he is not good, regret will have no reach.
translations.idiomatic: A child on the throne is a gamble—if he turns vicious, remorse will come too late.

sentences.zh: 時太后及冀貪立年幼，欲久自傳，遂立質帝，八岁。

translations.literal: At that time the empress dowager and Ji greedily established one who was young, wishing to prolong their own transmission; thereupon they set up Emperor Zhi, eight years old.
translations.idiomatic: The dowager and Liang Ji preferred a malleable child so they could prolong their regency, and enthroned the eight-year-old Emperor Zhi.

sentences.zh: 此不用德。

translations.literal: This was not using virtue.
translations.idiomatic: They spurned the counsel of virtue.

sentences.zh: 桓帝元嘉元年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Huandi's first year of Yuanjia, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Huan's first Yuanjia summer was dry.

sentences.zh: 是時，梁冀秉政，妻、子並受封，寵逾節。

translations.literal: At that time Liang Ji held power; wife and sons together received enfeoffment; favor exceeded measure.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji dominated the court while his wife and sons piled up titles beyond all decency.

sentences.zh: 延熹元年六月，旱。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yanxi, sixth month, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: The sixth month of Yanxi 1 saw drought.

sentences.zh: 靈帝熹平五年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In Lingdi's fifth year of Xiping, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling's fifth Xiping summer brought drought.

sentences.zh: 六年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the sixth year, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: The following summer was dry as well.

sentences.zh: 光和五年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the fifth year of Guanghe, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: Guanghe 5 opened with a drought summer.

sentences.zh: 六年夏，旱。

translations.literal: In the sixth year, summer, there was drought.
translations.idiomatic: The next year the same scourge returned.

sentences.zh: 是時，常侍、黄門僭作威福。

translations.literal: At that time regular attendants and yellow-gate eunuchs usurped making awesomeness and blessings.
translations.idiomatic: Palace eunuchs were then playing tyrant, handing down fortune and ruin at whim.

sentences.zh: 獻帝興平元年秋，長安旱。

translations.literal: In Xiandi's first year of Xingping, autumn, Chang'an had drought.
translations.idiomatic: Chang'an withered in the autumn of Xingping 1 under Emperor Xian.

sentences.zh: 是時，李傕、郭汜專權縱事。

translations.literal: At that time Li Jue and Guo Si monopolized power and gave free rein to affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Li Jue and Guo Si then ran the capital as they pleased.

sentences.zh: 更始時，南陽有童謠曰：「諧不諧，在赤眉。

translations.literal: In Gengshi's time, Nanyang had a children's song saying: "Harmonious or not harmonious, lies with the Red Eyebrows."
translations.idiomatic: During the Gengshi interregnum a rhyme ran through Nanyang: "Whether the tune holds—ask the Red Eyebrows."

sentences.zh: 得不得，在河北。

translations.literal: Obtaining or not obtaining, lies with Hebei.
translations.idiomatic: "Whether the prize is won—look to the north of the Yellow River."

sentences.zh: 」是時，更始在長安，世祖爲大司馬平定河北。

translations.literal: " At this time Gengshi was in Chang'an; Shizu was grand marshal pacifying Hebei.
translations.idiomatic: Gengshi held Chang'an while Liu Xiu, as grand marshal, was pacifying the north.

sentences.zh: 更始大臣並僭專權，故謠妖作也。

translations.literal: Gengshi's great ministers together usurped sole power; therefore song prodigies arose.
translations.idiomatic: Gengshi's ministers had all seized power beyond their right—hence these portentous rhymes.

sentences.zh: 后更始遂爲赤眉所殺，是更始之不諧在赤眉也。

translations.literal: Later Gengshi was then killed by the Red Eyebrows; this was Gengshi's lack of harmony lying with the Red Eyebrows.
translations.idiomatic: The Red Eyebrows soon killed Gengshi—the "lack of harmony" line had pointed straight at them.

sentences.zh: 世祖自河北興。

translations.literal: Shizu rose from Hebei.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xiu rose to power from the Hebei plain.

sentences.zh: 世祖建武六年，蜀童謠曰：「黄牛白腹，五铢當復。

translations.literal: In Shizu's sixth year of Jianwu, Shu had a children's song saying: "Yellow ox, white belly; the five-zhu coin ought to return."
translations.idiomatic: In Jianwu 6 a Shu children's rhyme ran: "The yellow bull shows a white belly—the Han five-zhu coin will return."

sentences.zh: 」是時，公孙述僭號於蜀，時人窃言王莽称黄，述欲继之，故称白；

translations.literal: " At this time Gongsun Shu usurped title in Shu; people of the time secretly said Wang Mang was called yellow, Shu wished to succeed him, therefore called white;
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Shu had declared himself emperor in Shu; gossips said Wang Mang's regime had been the "yellow" phase and Shu styled itself "white" as his successor;

sentences.zh: 五铢，漢家货，明當復也。

translations.literal: the five-zhu is Han house currency; clearly it ought to return.
translations.idiomatic: the five-zhu was Han coinage—plainly it would be restored.

sentences.zh: 述遂誅滅。

translations.literal: Shu was then executed and destroyed.
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Shu was destroyed.

sentences.zh: 王莽末，天水童謠曰：「出吳門，望缇羣。

translations.literal: At the end of Wang Mang, Tianshui had a children's song saying: "Go out the Wu Gate, gaze at the Ti herd."
translations.idiomatic: Near Wang Mang's fall Tianshui children sang: "Out through Wu Gate, eyes on the Ti hills."

sentences.zh: 見一蹇人，言欲上天；

translations.literal: Seeing one lame man, he says he wishes to ascend Heaven;
translations.idiomatic: "There walks a cripple who swears he will climb to Heaven;"

sentences.zh: 令天可上，地上安得民！

translations.literal: supposing Heaven could be ascended, how could there be people on earth!
translations.idiomatic: "If Heaven were truly within reach, what people would be left on earth!"

sentences.zh: 」時，隗嚣初起兵於天水，后意稍廣，欲爲天子，遂破滅，嚣少病蹇。

translations.literal: " At that time Wei Xiao first raised troops in Tianshui; later his intent gradually broadened, he wished to be Son of Heaven, thereupon was destroyed and perished; Xiao in youth had been ill with lameness.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Xiao had launched his rebellion from Tianshui, then dreamed of the throne—and fell; he had been lame from youth, matching the rhyme's cripple.

sentences.zh: 吳門，冀郭門名也。

translations.literal: Wu Gate is the name of a Ji city gate.
translations.idiomatic: "Wu Gate" was a gate in the Ji capital's wall.

sentences.zh: 缇羣，山名也。

translations.literal: Ti herd is a mountain name.
translations.idiomatic: "Ti herd" denoted a mountain.

sentences.zh: 順帝之末，京都童謠曰：「直如弦，死道邊。

translations.literal: At the end of Shundi, the capital had a children's song saying: "Straight as a bowstring—dead beside the road."
translations.idiomatic: Late in Emperor Shun's reign Luoyang children chanted: "Straight as a bowstring—you end dead in the ditch."

sentences.zh: 曲如鈎，反封侯。

translations.literal: Curved like a hook—on the contrary enfeoffed marquis.
translations.idiomatic: "Crooked as a fishhook—you win a marquisate instead."

sentences.zh: 」案順帝即世，孝質短祚，大將軍梁冀貪树疏幼，以爲己功，專國號令，以赡其私。

translations.literal: " Examining: when Shundi passed from the world, Xiaozhi had a short reign; the great general Liang Ji greedily set up a distant youth, taking it as his own merit, monopolized state commands, so as to enrich his private interests.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Shun died; Emperor Zhi reigned briefly; Liang Ji the general-in-chief forced a distant child onto the throne, claimed the credit, and bent every edict to private gain.

sentences.zh: 太尉李固以爲清河王雅性聪明，敦詩悦禮，加又属亲，立長則順，置善則固。

translations.literal: Grand Commandant Li Gu considered that the Prince of Qinghe by nature was intelligent, earnest in the Odes and pleased with the Rites, moreover was of kin by category; establishing the elder then is compliant, setting the good then is firm.
translations.idiomatic: Li Gu urged enthroning the Prince of Qinghe—a clever, cultivated kinsman; the elder line would satisfy the realm, a worthy choice would steady the state.

sentences.zh: 而冀建白太后，策免固，征蠡吾侯，遂即至尊。

translations.literal: But Ji memorialized the empress dowager, ordered dismissal of Gu, summoned the marquis of Liwu, thereupon he ascended the supreme seat.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji overruled him, secured the dowager's edict, cashiered Li Gu, and brought in the Marquis of Liwu—the future Emperor Huan.

sentences.zh: 固是日幽毙於獄，暴尸道路，而太尉胡廣封安樂乡侯、司徒趙戒厨亭侯、司空袁湯安國亭侯云。

translations.literal: Gu that day was secretly killed in prison, his corpse exposed on the road, while Grand Commandant Hu Guang was enfeoffed marquis of Anle township, Minister of Education Zhao Jie marquis of Chuting pavilion, Minister of Works Yuan Tang marquis of Anguo pavilion, and so on.
translations.idiomatic: Li Gu died the same day in a dungeon, his body flung in the street, while Hu Guang, Zhao Jie, and Yuan Tang—the ministers who bent to Liang Ji—each walked away with a new noble title.

sentences.zh: 桓帝之初，天下童謠曰：「小麦青青大麦枯，誰當獲者婦與姑。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Huandi, all under Heaven had a children's song saying: "The wheat is green-green, the barley withered; who shall reap—women and mothers-in-law."
translations.idiomatic: Early in Emperor Huan's reign a rhyme swept the empire: "Green wheat, blasted barley—who gathers the harvest? Wives and mothers-in-law."

sentences.zh: 丈人何在西击胡，吏買馬，君具車，請爲諸君鼓咙胡。

translations.literal: Why is the old man in the west striking the Hu; clerks buy horses, you prepare the carts; I beg to for you all beat the throat Hu.
translations.idiomatic: "Where are the men? Off west fighting the Hu; clerks must buy horses, masters fit the carts—let me hum a marching tune for you all."

sentences.zh: 」案元嘉中凉州諸羌一時俱反，南入蜀、漢，東抄三輔，延及並、冀，大爲民害。

translations.literal: " Examining: in the Yuanjia period the various Qiang of Liangzhou together at one time all rebelled, entered south into Shu and Han, raided east the Three Adjuncts, extended to Bing and Ji, greatly becoming harm to the people.
translations.idiomatic: In the Yuanjia years the Liangzhou Qiang revolted as one, poured into Ba and Han, pillaged the capital region, and spread ruin through Bing and Ji.

sentences.zh: 命將出眾，每戰常负，中國益发甲卒，麦多委棄，但有婦女獲刈之也。

translations.literal: Ordered generals went out with hosts; in each battle they constantly lost; the central states ever more sent armored soldiers; much wheat was cast aside and abandoned; only there were women who reaped and cut it.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial armies marched and lost again and again; conscripts multiplied while grain rotted in the fields—only women were left to scythe what they could.

sentences.zh: 吏買馬，君具車者，言调发重及有秩者也。

translations.literal: "Clerks buy horses, you prepare carts" means speaking of heavy levies reaching those with rank.
translations.idiomatic: The line about clerks, horses, and masters' carts meant crushing levies on every salaried official.

sentences.zh: 請爲諸君鼓咙胡者，不敢公言，私咽語。

translations.literal: "I beg to for you all beat the throat Hu" means not daring to speak openly, privately swallowing words.
translations.idiomatic: "Let me hum for you" meant the people dared not speak aloud and muttered their grievances in their throats.

sentences.zh: 桓帝之初，京都童謠曰：「城上烏，尾畢逋，公爲吏，子爲徒。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Huandi, the capital had a children's song saying: "The crow on the wall, tail all scattered; the father is clerk, the son is convict laborer."
translations.idiomatic: Another Luoyang rhyme in Emperor Huan's early years ran: "Crows on the city wall, tails all frayed—fathers turned clerks, sons turned convicts."

sentences.zh: 一徒死，百乘車。

translations.literal: One convict laborer dies, a hundred carriages.
translations.idiomatic: "One conscript dies—a hundred carriages roll."

sentences.zh: 車班班，入河間。

translations.literal: Carriages in rows, enter Hejian.
translations.idiomatic: "Carriages in long lines—winding their way to Hejian."

sentences.zh: 河間姹女工數錢，以錢爲室金爲堂。

translations.literal: The Hejian beauty is skilled at counting cash; she takes cash for chamber and gold for hall.
translations.idiomatic: "The Hejian belle counts her coins—rooms built of copper cash, halls sheeted in gold."

sentences.zh: 石上慊慊舂黄粱。

translations.literal: On the stone, sorrowfully pounding yellow millet.
translations.idiomatic: "On the stone mortar, pestles thump—only yellow millet left to grind."

sentences.zh: 梁下有悬鼓，我欲击之丞卿怒。

translations.literal: Beneath the beam hangs a drum; I wish to strike it, but the assistant minister and chief ministers grow angry.
translations.idiomatic: A line from the rhyme: "There's a petition drum under the rafters—I reach for the mallet, but the chancellor and his men fly into a rage."

sentences.zh: 」案此皆謂爲政貪也。

translations.literal: " Examining: all these are said to mean grasping greed in government.
translations.idiomatic: The commentary takes every image in that song as a verdict on rapacious rule.

sentences.zh: 城上烏，尾畢逋者，處高利独食，不與下共，謂人主多聚敛也。

translations.literal: "The crow on the wall, tail all scattered" means occupying high profit and eating alone, not sharing with those below; it speaks of the ruler greatly amassing revenue.
translations.idiomatic: The rooftop crow hoarding scraps alone foretells a Son of Heaven who squeezes the realm for revenue and shares nothing downward.

sentences.zh: 公爲吏，子爲徒者，言蛮夷將叛逆，父既爲軍吏，其子又爲卒徒往击之也。

translations.literal: "The father is clerk, the son convict laborer" means the barbarians will rebel; the father having already been a military clerk, his son again becomes foot-soldier and convict laborer to go strike them.
translations.idiomatic: Fathers pressed into the army clerks' corps and sons dragooned as convict troops point to frontier revolts that devour one generation after another.

sentences.zh: 一徒死，百乘車者，言前一人往討胡既死矣，后又遣百乘車往。

translations.literal: "One convict laborer dies, a hundred carriages" means the first man sent to punish the Hu already died, afterward again a hundred carriages were dispatched.
translations.idiomatic: One expeditionary column perishes; the court answers by flinging a hundred more chariots into the same meat grinder.

sentences.zh: 車班班，入河間者，言上將崩，乘舆班班入河間迎靈帝也。

translations.literal: "Carriages in rows, enter Hejian" means the sovereign is about to die; imperial carriages in rows enter Hejian to welcome Emperor Ling.
translations.idiomatic: The long train rolling toward Hejian foretold the emperor's death and the hearse-road that would bring the boy Liu Hong from Hejian to the throne.

sentences.zh: 河間姹女工數錢，以錢爲室金爲堂者，靈帝既立，其母永樂太后好聚金以爲堂也。

translations.literal: "The Hejian beauty skilled at counting cash, taking cash for chamber and gold for hall" means after Ling was established, his mother Empress Dowager Yongle loved amassing gold to build halls.
translations.idiomatic: The miserly belle piling coins into walls of copper and ceilings of gold stood for Lady Dong of Yongle, who hoarded specie to gild her palace halls once her son sat on the throne.

sentences.zh: 石上慊慊舂黄粱者，言永樂雖积金錢，慊慊常苦不足，使人舂黄粱而食之也。

translations.literal: "Sorrowfully pounding yellow millet on the stone" means although Yongle piled gold and cash, she sorrowfully always suffered insufficiency, and had people pound yellow millet and eat it.
translations.idiomatic: The pestle on the mortar meant that even mountains of gold could not sate her—she still grudged every grain and made servants pound millet as if famine stalked the harem.

sentences.zh: 梁下有悬鼓，我欲击之丞卿怒者，言永樂主教靈帝，使卖官受錢，所祿非其人，天下忠笃之士怨望，欲击悬鼓以求見，丞卿主鼓者，亦復谄順，怒而止我也。

translations.literal: "Beneath the beam hangs a drum; I wish to strike it, but the assistant minister and chief ministers grow angry" means Yongle instructed Ling to sell offices and receive money, so that salaries went to unworthy men; loyal and sincere knights of the realm resented and wished to strike the hanging drum to seek audience; the assistant and minister in charge of the drum likewise flattered and yielded and angrily stopped them.
translations.idiomatic: The blocked drumbeat pictured honest men who wished to pound the grievance drum only to find the Yongle faction—having taught the emperor to vend offices—had bribed every gatekeeper; the very officials who should relay petitions silenced them instead.

sentences.zh: 桓帝之初，京都童謠曰：「游平卖印自有平，不辟豪賢及大姓。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Huandi, the capital had a children's song saying: "You Ping sells seals and there is peace; it does not avoid powerful worthies and great clans."
translations.idiomatic: Another capital rhyme at the start of Emperor Huan's reign ran: "You Ping vends the seals—and balance returns; he shows no favor to magnates or great houses."

sentences.zh: 」案到延熹之末，鄧皇后以譴自殺，乃以竇貴人代之，其父名武字游平，拜城門校尉。

translations.literal: " Examining: when it reached the end of Yanxi, Empress Deng by reproach committed suicide, then the Honored Lady Dou was substituted; her father was named Wu, style You Ping, and was appointed colonel of the city gates.
translations.idiomatic: By late Yanxi Empress Deng had been forced to suicide; Honored Lady Dou replaced her. Her father Dou Wu, whose courtesy name was You Ping, became colonel of the city gates—the very "You Ping" of the rhyme.

sentences.zh: 及太后攝政，爲大將軍，與太傅陳蕃合心戮力，惟德是建，印綬所加，咸得其人，豪賢大姓，皆絕望矣。

translations.literal: When the empress dowager held the regency, he became great general; with grand tutor Chen Fan he united hearts and joined strength; only virtue was established; wherever seals and ribbons were bestowed, all obtained the right men; powerful worthies and great clans were all cut off from hope.
translations.idiomatic: Under the regency Dou Wu served as general-in-chief beside Grand Tutor Chen Fan; together they handed offices only to worthy men, slamming the door on every great clan that had bought favor under the Liangs.

sentences.zh: 桓帝之末，京都童謠曰：「茅田一頃中有井，四方纤纤不可整。

translations.literal: At the end of Huandi, the capital had a children's song saying: "A thatched field of one qing has a well in it; on four sides, fine and fine, it cannot be set straight."
translations.idiomatic: Late in Emperor Huan's reign Luoyang sang: "A hempfield of one qing with a well at its heart—ragged on every side, beyond all mending."

sentences.zh: 嚼復嚼，今年尚可后年鐃。

translations.literal: Chew again, chew again; this year is still tolerable, next year the nao bells.
translations.idiomatic: "Chew and chew—this year we scrape by; next year they'll beat the warning bells."

sentences.zh: 」案《易》曰：「拔茅茹以其汇，征吉。

translations.literal: " Examining the Changes, it says: "Pull up the rush by its roots, with its kind; the expedition is auspicious."
translations.idiomatic: The Classic of Changes counsels: "Uproot the reed and its runners together—then the campaign is lucky."

sentences.zh: 」茅喻羣賢也。

translations.literal: " Rush stands for the host of worthies.
translations.idiomatic: Here the reed patch stands for the cluster of honest ministers.

sentences.zh: 井者，法也。

translations.literal: The well means law.
translations.idiomatic: The well in the field is the standard of law still holding at the center.

sentences.zh: 於時中常侍管霸、苏康憎疾海内英哲，與長樂少府劉嚣、太常許咏、尚書柳分、尋穆、史佟、司隸唐珍等，代作脣齒。

translations.literal: At that time palace attendants Guan Ba and Su Kang hated the outstanding wise of the seas; with junior privy treasurer of Changle Liu Ao, chamberlain for ceremonies Xu Yong, secretariat directors Liu Fen, Xun Mu, Shi Tong, metropolitan commandant Tang Zhen, and others, they substituted for one another as lips and teeth.
translations.idiomatic: Eunuchs Guan Ba and Su Kang loathed every upright scholar-official; with Liu Ao, Xu Yong, Liu Fen, Xun Mu, Shi Tong, Tang Zhen, and the rest they formed a ring of mutual cover like lip and teeth.

sentences.zh: 河内牢川詣闕上書：「汝、颍、南陽，上采虚誉，專作威福；

translations.literal: A man of Henei, Lao Chuan, went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial: "Runan, Yingchuan, and Nanyang upward gather empty reputation and exclusively make awesomeness and blessings;
translations.idiomatic: A certain Lao Chuan of Henei petitioned the throne: "Runan, Yingchuan, and Nanyang traffic in hollow fame and throw their weight about unchecked;

sentences.zh: 甘陵有南北二部，三輔尤甚。

translations.literal: Ganling has south and north factions; the Three Adjuncts are still worse."
translations.idiomatic: Ganling is split into rival southern and northern cliques, and the capital region is worse still."

sentences.zh: 」由是傳考黄門北寺，始見廢閣。

translations.literal: " Thereupon they transmitted for examination the Northern Office of the Yellow Gates, and for the first time saw dismissal and closure.
translations.idiomatic: The case was kicked to the eunuchs' North Prison; for the first time the full machinery of purge and prison came into view.

sentences.zh: 茅田一頃者，言羣賢眾多也。

translations.literal: "A thatched field of one qing" means the host of worthies is numerous.
translations.idiomatic: The wide hempfield meant many good men still stood in court.

sentences.zh: 中有井者，言雖厄窮，不失其法度也。

translations.literal: "Having a well in it" means although in straits, one does not lose one's measure of law.
translations.idiomatic: The well promised that even in distress the rule of law would not be lost.

sentences.zh: 四方纤纤不可整者，言姦慝大炽，不可整理。

translations.literal: "On four sides, fine and fine, it cannot be set straight" means treacherous wickedness blazes greatly and cannot be ordered.
translations.idiomatic: The frayed edges meant villainy had flared beyond correction.

sentences.zh: 嚼復嚼者，京都飲酒相強之辞也。

translations.literal: "Chew again, chew again" is the capital's phrase for pressing one another to drink.
translations.idiomatic: "Chew again" echoed the toasts by which Luoyang nobles bullied each other into another cup.

sentences.zh: 言食肉者鄙，不恤王政，徒耽宴飲歌呼而已也。

translations.literal: It means those who eat meat are base; they do not pity royal government, but only indulge in feasting, drinking, and shouting.
translations.idiomatic: It mocked meat-eating grandees who ignored the state and drowned only in banquet noise.

sentences.zh: 今年尚可者，言但禁錮也。

translations.literal: "This year is still tolerable" means only proscription.
translations.idiomatic: "This year we scrape by" meant the court still stopped at stripping offices—mere faction proscription.

sentences.zh: 后年鐃者，陳、竇被誅，天下大壞。

translations.literal: "Next year the nao bells" means Chen and Dou were executed and all under Heaven was greatly ruined.
translations.idiomatic: "Next year the bells" was the massacre of Chen Fan and Dou Wu and the collapse that followed.

sentences.zh: 桓帝之末，京都童謠曰：「白盖小車何延延。

translations.literal: At the end of Huandi, the capital had a children's song saying: "Little white-canopied carriages, how they stretch on and on."
translations.idiomatic: Another late-Huan rhyme went: "Little white-topped coaches—what an endless stream!"

sentences.zh: 河間來合諧，河間來合諧！

translations.literal: Hejian comes in harmony; Hejian comes in harmony!
translations.idiomatic: "From Hejian they come, all in tune—from Hejian they come, all in tune!"

sentences.zh: 」案解犊亭属饶陽河間县也。

translations.literal: " Examining: Jiedu Pavilion belongs to Raoyang in Hejian county.
translations.idiomatic: Jiedu Post stood in Raoyang county under Hejian—ground zero for the omen.

sentences.zh: 居无幾何而桓帝崩，使者與解犊侯皆白盖車從河間來。

translations.literal: Before long Huandi died; envoys and the marquis of Jiedu both rode white-canopied carts coming from Hejian.
translations.idiomatic: Within weeks Emperor Huan was dead; heralds and the Marquis of Jiedu rolled toward Luoyang in white-canopied wagons from Hejian.

sentences.zh: 延延，眾貌也。

translations.literal: Yanyan is the appearance of a crowd.
translations.idiomatic: Yanyan painted the long, crowded train of coaches.

sentences.zh: 是時御史劉儵建議立靈帝，以儵爲侍中，中常侍侯览畏其亲近，必當間己，白拜儵泰山太守，因令司隸迫促殺之。

translations.literal: At that time imperial secretary Liu You proposed establishing Emperor Ling; he was made palace attendant; palace attendant Hou Lan feared he would be intimate with the sovereign and would surely alienate himself from Lan, and so memorialized to appoint You grand administrator of Taishan, then ordered the Metropolitan Province to press and hurry and kill him.
translations.idiomatic: Liu You had urged Liu Hong's accession and won a palace post; Hou Lan, fearing a rival at the emperor's ear, had him packed off to Taishan and hounded to death by the metropolitan commandant.

sentences.zh: 朝廷少長，思其功效，乃拔用其弟郃，致位司徒，此爲合諧也。

translations.literal: The court, young and old, thought of his merit and effect; thereupon they promoted and used his younger brother He, reaching the position of minister of education; this was "coming in harmony."
translations.idiomatic: Courtiers remembered Liu You's service and raised his brother Liu He to minister of education—Hejian's "harmony" made good after all.

sentences.zh: 靈帝之末，京都童謠曰：「侯非侯，王非王，千乘萬騎上北芒。

translations.literal: At the end of Lingdi, the capital had a children's song saying: "He is no marquis, the king is no king; a thousand chariots and ten thousand riders ascend Beimang."
translations.idiomatic: As Emperor Ling's reign failed, children sang: "No lord is lord, no king is king—thousands of chariots climb Beimang Hill."

sentences.zh: 」案到中平六年，史侯登蹑至尊，獻帝未有爵號，爲中常侍段珪等數十人所執，公卿百官皆随其后，到河上，乃得來還。

translations.literal: " Examining: when it reached the sixth year of Zhongping, Marquis Shi mounted the supreme seat step by step; Emperor Xian had not yet a noble title; he was seized by several tens of persons including palace attendant Duan Gui; dukes, ministers, and all officials followed behind them; only when they reached the river were they able to return.
translations.idiomatic: In Zhongping 6 the young Liu Xie was hustled to the throne while his brother lacked even a princely rank; dozens of eunuchs led him off with the whole bureaucracy trailing until the party turned back only at the Yellow River.

sentences.zh: 此爲非侯非王上北芒者也。

translations.literal: This was "not marquis, not king, ascending Beimang."
translations.idiomatic: That was the scene the rhyme called "no marquis, no king, climbing Beimang."

sentences.zh: 靈帝中平中，京都歌曰：「承樂世董逃，游四郭董逃，蒙天恩董逃，带金紫董逃，行谢恩董逃，整車騎董逃，垂欲发董逃，與中辞董逃，出西門董逃，瞻宫殿董逃，望京城董逃，日夜絕董逃，心摧傷董逃。

translations.literal: In Lingdi's Zhongping era, the capital had a song saying: "Receiving happy times—Dong flees; roaming the four outer walls—Dong flees; receiving Heaven's grace—Dong flees; wearing gold and purple—Dong flees; walking to thank grace—Dong flees; arraying chariots and horse—Dong flees; about to set out—Dong flees; taking leave in the palace—Dong flees; going out the west gate—Dong flees; gazing at palace halls—Dong flees; looking at the capital city—Dong flees; day and night cut off—Dong flees; heart broken and wounded—Dong flees."
translations.idiomatic: Mid-Zhongping Luoyang took up a bitter refrain: every line of life's pomp ended in the refrain "Dong flees"—a drumbeat on the name Dong Zhuo.

sentences.zh: 」案「董」謂董卓也，言雖跋扈，縱其残暴，終歸逃窜，至於滅族也。

translations.literal: " Examining: "Dong" means Dong Zhuo; although he was domineering and let loose his cruelty and violence, in the end he fled and scattered until his clan was exterminated.
translations.idiomatic: The hidden word was Dong Zhuo: however he strutted, the song foretold he would end in flight and clan extinction.

sentences.zh: 獻帝践祚之初，京都童謠曰：「千里草，何青青。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Xiandi's treading the throne, the capital had a children's song saying: "Thousand-mile grass, how green-green."
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Xian first mounted the throne, Luoyang children chanted: "The grass that runs a thousand li—how lush and green!"

sentences.zh: 十日卜，不得生。

translations.literal: Ten days divination—cannot obtain life.
translations.idiomatic: "Ten days atop the divination sign—no survivor below."

sentences.zh: 」案千里草爲董，十日卜爲卓。

translations.literal: " Examining: "thousand-mile grass" makes Dong; "ten days" atop "divination" makes Zhuo.
translations.idiomatic: Read as a riddle, the lines stack into the characters for Dong Zhuo.

sentences.zh: 凡别字之體，皆從上起，左右离合，无有從下发端者也。

translations.literal: In general the form of variant-character riddles all begins from the top, left and right joining and separating; there is none that begins from the bottom issuing upward.
translations.idiomatic: Charade characters normally stack from the top outward; none start from the bottom and climb—

sentences.zh: 今二字如此者，天意若曰：卓自下摩上，以臣陵君也。

translations.literal: Now that the two characters are thus, Heaven's intent was as if saying: Zhuo from below rubs upward, using minister to encroach on lord.
translations.idiomatic: —so Heaven arranged the pieces to show Zhuo thrusting upward from below, a subject bullying his sovereign.

sentences.zh: 青青者，暴盛之貌也。

translations.literal: Green-green is the appearance of violent flourishing.
translations.idiomatic: "Green-green" pictured his swagger at its height.

sentences.zh: 不得生者，亦旋破亡。

translations.literal: "Cannot obtain life" means likewise soon destroyed and perished.
translations.idiomatic: "No survivor below" meant he would soon be destroyed.

sentences.zh: 建安初，荆州童謠曰：「八九年間始欲衰，至十三年无孑遺。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Jian'an, Jingzhou had a children's song saying: "Between eight and nine years it first begins to decline; by the thirteenth year not a sprig is left."
translations.idiomatic: Early in Jian'an a Jingzhou rhyme warned: "Around the eighth or ninth year the bloom fades; by the thirteenth nothing remains."

sentences.zh: 」言自中興以來，荆州无破亂，及劉表爲牧，民又豐樂，至此逮八九年。

translations.literal: " It means from the restoration onward Jingzhou had not been broken in disorder, and when Liu Biao became shepherd the people were again abundant and happy; here it reached eight or nine years.
translations.idiomatic: Since the Guangwu restoration Jingzhou had known peace; under Liu Biao the people prospered—for about eight or nine years.

sentences.zh: 當始衰者，謂劉表妻當死，諸將並零落也。

translations.literal: "When it first declines" means Liu Biao's wife was about to die, and the various generals together fell away scattered.
translations.idiomatic: "Begins to decline" foretold Lady Cai's death and the scattering of Biao's generals.

sentences.zh: 十三年无孑遺者，言十三年表又當死，民當移詣冀州也。

translations.literal: "By the thirteenth year not a sprig is left" means in the thirteenth year Biao again was about to die, and the people were about to shift to Ji Province.
translations.idiomatic: The thirteenth year marked Liu Biao's own end and the people's removal toward the north under Cao Cao's Ji Province.

sentences.zh: 順帝陽嘉元年十月中，望都蒲陰狼殺童兒九十七人。

translations.literal: In the tenth month of the first year of Yangjia under Shundi, in Wangdu and Puyin wolves killed ninety-seven children.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month of Yangjia 1 wolves slaughtered ninety-seven children in Wangdu and Puyin.

sentences.zh: 時，李固对策，引京房《易傳》曰「君將无道，害將及人，去之深山以全身，厥妖狼食人」。

translations.literal: At that time Li Gu in his examination answer cited Jing Fang's Commentary on the Changes: "When the lord is about to be without the Way, harm will reach men; leave for deep mountains to preserve the whole body; its prodigy is wolves devouring people."
translations.idiomatic: Li Gu quoted Jing Fang: "When the ruler loses the Way, disaster reaches the people—flee to the hills; Heaven sends wolves to devour them."

sentences.zh: 陛下覺寤，比求隱滞，故狼災息。

translations.literal: Your Majesty awoke and compared, seeking the hidden and stuck; therefore wolf disaster ceased.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor took the hint, sought out neglected talent, and the wolf scourge—so the memorial claimed—abated.

sentences.zh: 靈帝建寧中，羣狼數十頭入晉陽南城門嚙人。

translations.literal: In Lingdi's Jianning era, a pack of several tens of wolves entered the south gate of Jinyang and bit people.
translations.idiomatic: During Jianning a pack of wolves burst through Jinyang's south gate and mauled townsfolk.
